name: Frailty — provider-side Medicaid exemption desk
one_liner: For the operations director of a community mental health center, opioid treatment program or FQHC, Frailty finds which of their Medicaid patients are about to be hit by the January 2027 work-reporting rule, assembles a state-specific "medically frail" exemption packet from the chart, and routes it to a clinician for a one-click signature.
problem: From 1 January 2027, most Medicaid expansion adults aged 19-64 must document 80 hours a month of work/school/volunteering every six months, or qualify for an exemption. CMS's interim final rule makes the "medically frail" exclusion a two-part test: a qualifying condition (SUD, serious mental illness, disabling condition, complex medical condition) AND evidence that it significantly impairs the person's ability to comply. States must check their own data first; when data doesn't settle it, the member gets a noncompliance notice and ~30 days to produce proof — and in practice they walk into their clinic and ask the front desk for a letter. Kentucky already publishes a clinician-signed exemption form (MACE-200) and accepts a signed letter on provider letterhead; SHVS's October 2026 state readiness roadmap tells states that will not accept self-attestation in 2027 to finalise standardised provider attestation forms. Self-attestation is further restricted from 2028. Safety-net clinics have no system for this: today it is a case manager pulling the chart, a clinician writing freehand prose that may not address the functional-impairment test, a fax or portal upload, and no tracking of the 30-day clock or the 12-month re-verification. When the letter is late or weak, the patient loses coverage and the clinic loses the revenue and often keeps treating them.
target_customer: Operations/compliance director or CFO of a safety-net behavioural health provider in a Medicaid expansion state: CCBHCs (495 clinics across 46 states + DC + PR as of March 2024, ~3M clients), opioid treatment programs (SAMHSA lists 2,112 programs; >600k patients/year, roughly ~300 patients per program; one study estimates ~75% of OTP patients have Medicaid), and FQHC behavioural health lines. These organisations have a named budget owner, already buy per-clinician SaaS add-ons, and their entire payer mix is the exposed population. Buyer is the ops/compliance director; the economic argument goes to the CFO.
why_now: A hard, dated deadline: the federal community-engagement requirement applies no later than 1 January 2027, with Nebraska, Montana, Arkansas and Iowa already in soft or full implementation during 2026 (https://www.kff.org/medicaid/medicaid-work-requirements-tracker-state-national-data-and-policies/). CBO projects ~5.3M more uninsured by 2034; Urban estimates ~3.1M fewer Medicaid enrollees in the first full year (https://www.urban.org/research/publication/new-federal-rule-medicaid-work-requirements-understates-likely-coverage-losses). CMS's June 2026 IFR narrowed "medically frail" to a two-part functional test (https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/medicaid-community-engagement-requirement-certain-individuals-interim-final-rule-comment-period-cms), and SHVS's 8 Oct 2026 roadmap pushes states to publish standardised provider attestation forms (https://shvs.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Medicaid-WRRs_State-Readiness-Roadmap-10.08.2026.pdf). Self-attestation is allowed broadly only through 2027, so provider documentation becomes the main route in 2028. This maps directly onto YC's [latest] RFS "Plaid for Government Benefits" (Gustaf Alströmer, https://www.ycombinator.com/rfs#plaid-for-government-benefits) and a16z's "Vertical AI evolves ... to multiplayer" (https://a16z.com/newsletter/big-ideas-2026-part-1/) — but from the provider side, which both describe only obliquely. Technically, long-context models that can read a messy chart and produce a criteria-mapped narrative are what make a 2-minute packet possible; that is a 2025-26 capability.
comparables: Fortuna Health (fortunahealth.com) — Medicaid enrollment/renewal navigation sold to plans and providers, $22M raised ($4M seed + $18M Series A led by a16z Bio+Health), partners include Highmark Wholecare, MVP, Cedar, R1; it guides the *member* through applications, logs and documents. It does not produce the clinician-signed, criteria-mapped medical-frailty packet. Healthy Together and Vimo (Medicaid Express "Community Engagement as a Service") — member/state-facing hour logging and exemption screening, per CBPP's vendor landscape (https://www.cbpp.org/research/health/assessing-the-medicaid-work-requirement-vendor-landscape); again member- and state-side, not provider-side. Centauri Health Solutions, Ushur, mPulse, Pointcare, Relay — payer-side retention and redetermination outreach; they contact members, they do not touch the chart or the clinician signature. Deloitte and the state eligibility integrators build the state's verification engine, the other side of the same transaction. The gap I found, and which an independent analyst states plainly (https://www.onhealthcare.tech/p/the-exemption-machine-part-two-building): the clinical layer — the tier of cases where a licensed clinician must review evidence and attest — is unserved, and no vendor I could find sells an EHR/claims-driven provider exemption documentation product. I did not find a product occupying this slot; I may have missed a quiet one.
market_note: Estimate, clearly labelled: ~2,100 OTPs + ~495 CCBHCs + ~1,400 FQHC organisations gives roughly 4,000 US safety-net sites in expansion states as an addressable base. At $800-$2,500/clinic/month (in line with published behavioural-health SaaS add-on pricing of $35-$150 per clinician per month and usage-based claim pricing from ~$0.38/claim), that is a $40-120M ARR ceiling on the narrow wedge — enough for a real company, and the natural expansions (SNAP ABAWD exemptions, disability paperwork, prior-auth letters, 12-month re-verification) are the same muscle. Willingness to pay is anchored not on software budgets but on retained revenue: health centres earn roughly $1,609 in Medicaid revenue per Medicaid patient per year (KFF 2025, health centres overall — not BH-specific), and Medicare's OTP weekly methadone bundle is $277.29, so a single retained patient-year is worth four figures. Keeping 20 patients covered pays for the product many times over. All sizing here is my estimate from the counts cited, not a vendor figure.
risks: 1) States may verify most frail patients automatically from claims and BH encounter data (San Diego's DMC-ODS training already says qualifying BH data in state systems makes someone exempt), shrinking the manual-packet volume to a tail — though a tail of 5-15% of millions is still large. 2) Provider liability and advocacy pushback: medical associations have objected to putting clinicians in the position of deciding coverage, and some clinics may refuse to systematise attestations. 3) Policy risk: litigation, a delay to the 1 Jan 2027 date, or a state-by-state retreat would deflate the deadline that powers the whole wedge. 4) Fifty-state fragmentation — each state's form, criteria tier and submission channel differs, so the build is configuration-heavy; mitigated by starting in two or three states.
riskiest_assumptions: Most fragile first: (a) that a meaningful share of exempt patients will NOT be caught by the state's automated data match, so clinics actually receive a stream of letter requests — I found the policy structure that creates this but no volume data; (b) that the clinic, not the health plan or the state, is the one who pays — plans have deeper pockets and Fortuna already sells there, so the clinic wedge must survive a "why doesn't the MCO buy this" test; (c) that a clinician will sign an AI-assembled packet, i.e. that the draft is trusted enough to cut review to minutes rather than adding a review burden.
first_customers: Ten named sites, reachable this month: CCBHCs and OTPs in Kentucky (MACE-200 is live and published), Montana and Nebraska (already enforcing), plus Louisiana and Iowa (Dec 1 start). Find them through the SAMHSA OTP directory, the National Council for Mental Wellbeing's CCBHC Success Center member list, and state primary care associations — each state PCA runs an HR1 implementation workgroup that is currently the single highest-density room of these buyers. Warm path: the National Council and NAATP conference circuits, and state behavioural health association listservs where clinics are already asking each other "what do we do when a patient asks for a frailty letter?"
validation_test: This week: email or call 15 CCBHC/OTP operations directors in KY, MT and NE with one question — "since the work rules started, how many patients have asked your clinicians for a medically-frail letter, who writes it, and how long does it take?" Then show five of them a single hard-coded screen: patient chart in, Kentucky MACE-200-shaped packet out with the functional-impairment paragraph pre-written and citations to the chart. Pass = at least 3 of 15 report they are already fielding requests with no process, AND at least 2 confirm in writing they would pay $1,000+/month, or sign a paid pilot LOI, before 1 January. Fail = clinics say the state is handling it automatically and nobody is asking them for letters; then the idea moves to the payer or the state side and the clinic wedge dies.
build_plan: Narrowest first version, one state (Kentucky), one form (MACE-200 provider version), no EHR integration. 1) Encode Kentucky's criteria and CMS's two-part test as a rules sheet: qualifying condition list + the functional-impairment question the letter must answer. 2) Ingest: let the clinic drop a CSV of active patients (age, payer, primary/secondary dx, last visit) or paste a chart summary — no FHIR, no HL7 in v1. 3) Risk list: flag patients 19-64 on Medicaid expansion with a qualifying dx and rank by likelihood the state's data match will miss them. 4) Packet generator: a long-context model drafts the MACE-200 fields and the letterhead narrative, every clinical statement linked to the source line in the chart, with the functional-impairment paragraph written to the state's language. 5) Clinician queue: a 60-second review-and-sign screen; export a PDF plus a submission checklist for the state's channel. 6) Clock: track the 30-day cure deadline per patient and the 12-month re-verification. Cut from v1: EHR write-back, e-signature compliance infra beyond a signed PDF, multi-state configuration, member-facing app, hour logging (that's Fortuna's and Healthy Together's lane), and any claim that the product determines eligibility — it never does; the state decides.
launch_post: Medicaid work rules hit Jan 1. Millions who qualify for the medically-frail exemption will lose coverage because nobody wrote the letter. Frailty turns a patient's chart into a state-ready exemption packet your clinician signs in 60 seconds. Starting with Kentucky's MACE-200.
reasoning:
Frailty won because it is the only candidate where a legally dated event forces a specific person to do a specific piece of paperwork they have no system for, and where my research actually found the seam rather than assuming it. Everything in the Medicaid work-requirement space is being built on two ends — member navigation (Fortuna, Healthy Together, Vimo) and state eligibility verification (Deloitte and the integrators) — while the middle, the clinician who must review evidence and attest that a condition significantly impairs the patient's ability to work, has no product. CMS's June 2026 rule made that a two-part functional test rather than a code lookup, which is precisely the kind of judgement a long-context model can draft and a clinician can approve in under a minute. The deadline is 1 Jan 2027, three states are already enforcing, and self-attestation narrows from 2028 — so the need grows rather than evaporates after launch.

It beat the deal-desk and agent-permissions finalists on gap and timing: both of those had plausible buyers, but CPQ incumbents already sell the deal-desk workflow, and agentic identity is a forming category with funded players and too much overlap with past ideas Proofline and Holdroom. Frailty does not repeat anything in the library; the closest past entries are Receipts (medical billing evidence records, different buyer and different workflow) and Compactly (nurse credentials, a consumer tool).

Honest caveats. Pain is 8, not 9: I confirmed the structure of the burden and that Kentucky already publishes a clinician form, but I found no measured volume of letter requests, no staffing numbers, and no behavioural-health-specific cost of a lost patient. Market_pull is 7 for the same reason — the role and the price points are real, but I have no buyer saying yes. And the whole thing rests on states not auto-exempting most frail patients from claims data; the week-one validation test is designed to kill it fast if they do. For this builder the fit is good on the automation and agent side and weak on healthcare access: he will need a clinical advisor and a design partner before writing much code, which is why effort is 3+ months rather than weeks.

Runner-up (Project, 7.6): Tonight's bookmark set is overwhelmingly launch videos — six of ten posts are screen recordings shipped the same day they were made. That is the tell: the audience in these bookmarks produces exactly the artefact Shiproom checks, which makes distribution trivial (scan their own public videos and reply). It beat the other candidates on three counts. Against the skill/agent-tooling candidates (2, 10) it isn't a repeat: past ideas Shelf and Skillscope already own the SKILL.md-paste workflow for the same audience, and Shiproom's input (a video file), audience (anyone posting a demo) and output (a blurred file) share nothing with them. Against the people-data candidates (3) it avoids both the $2.50/lookup wall and the overlap with tonight's data-heavy venture. Against the pure-model toys (4, 5) it has a reason to exist after the novelty: you run it before every launch, not once. It also differs from tonight's venture pick Frailty entirely — different people, different problem, different workflow. could_grow is true because the obvious next step is a team version that gates Loom/Cap exports before they leave an org, which is the "employees shipping things themselves" surface a16z's CISO survey says is the fastest-growing 2027 priority. The honest ceiling is 7.6, not 9: shareability is the weak leg — people will share their findings, but a redacted video is by definition something you share *instead of* the scan, and I could not find evidence of similar scans spreading before. I did not inflate it.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Frailty — provider-side Medicaid medically-frail exemption packets for CCBHCs/OTPs. PICK. Dated deadline, named buyer, confirmed unserved layer between member navigators and state eligibility engines.
2. Ploid-powered "who is this person really" KYC/KYA layer for agent payments (from @m9rcn + a16z KYA big idea). Dropped at screen — infrastructure play, crowded with funded identity vendors, no specific buyer with a budget line the builder could reach.
3. Lead-waterfall cost governor for RevOps (from @shengkunye's Jev post): route enrichment across Apollo/Clay/PDL and pay per kept lead. Dropped at screen — Jev itself is this, open source and free; cloning it fails the no-thin-variation rule.
4. Outbound-reply triage and spam-suppression layer for SMBs being carpet-bombed by Explee-style AI prospecting. Dropped at screen — buyer is the victim, not a budget holder; my search for expressed complaints returned nothing usable.
5. "AI laggard" token-and-adoption allocator for Heads of AI (from @businessbarista). Dropped at screen — crowded with Copilot adoption/shelfware analytics vendors (CloudNuro, LicenseIQ, VisualSP), and the honest version is an HR layoff tool the builder would not want to sell.
6. Deal Bot for the mid-market: non-standard contract terms detection and exception routing (from @bot's Shared Bots post). Finalist, lost. Real workflow, but CPQ/deal-desk incumbents (Salesforce Revenue Cloud, DealHub, Conga, Salesbricks) already route non-standard terms for exactly this buyer at a fair price; no confirmable gap and no deadline.
7. Internal AI-agent permission evidence pack for mid-market CISOs facing SOC 2 (from a16z's CISO survey: 46% worried about agents exceeding permissions, 45% plan to buy within 12 months). Finalist, lost. Strong timing and budget, but the "Okta + SailPoint for agents" category is already forming with funded entrants, and it is too close to past ideas Proofline and Holdroom in buyer and workflow.
8. On-device vertical inspection model packaging for field techs, riding LFM3's 1-GPU fine-tune and NPU targets. Dropped at screen — a capability in search of a buyer; the builder would be selling model ops to people who buy outcomes.
9. Permit correction-letter drafter for small building departments (YC "AI for City Hall"). Dropped at screen — CivCheck is already piloting with Honolulu and Seattle, Clariti distributes it, and municipal sales cycles are far too slow for an evenings-and-weekends founder to reach a first sale.
10. Hours-proof concierge for gig and shift workers subject to the same 2027 rule. Dropped at screen — consumer-side, no payer, and research confirmed employers have no new reporting duty, so there is no B2B hook.

PROJECT
1. Shiproom — pre-post leak scan for demo videos, fully in-browser with LFM3-VL + OCR. PICK: only candidate with a real (if latent) problem, a brand-new capability behind it, and an output that is both useful and postable.
2. Skill Diet Scoreboard — paste a SKILL.md, see its token cost and what a slimmed version would save. DROPPED AT SCREEN: too close to past ideas Shelf and Skillscope (same audience, same paste-a-SKILL.md workflow), and skill-diet itself already does the real version.
3. "What your agent sees" — paste your handle, Ploid/public-web data assembled into a profile card. DROPPED AT SCREEN: Ploid is $2.50 per person report with no usable free tier, and Whitebridge.ai plus a shelf of OSINT tools already do this; also creepy-adjacent and overlaps the venture's people-data theme.
4. Omni Memo — hum/talk at LFM3-Omni-2B in the browser, get structured typed output. DROPPED AT SCREEN: Omni's ONNX browser path isn't demonstrated yet (only VL has a working WebGPU space), so buildability was a coin flip.
5. Decision Desk — d1-2B typed decisions with calibrated probabilities over a pasted CSV. DROPPED AT SCREEN: genuinely fresh (YC's vertical-foundation-models signal points right at it) but the output is a probability table — nothing anyone screenshots, and no hosted free endpoint confirmed.
6. Laggard Mirror — paste your week's AI usage, see where you sit on the "10% do 90%" power law. DROPPED: the data is self-reported, so the output is fiction; also mean-spirited.
7. Patent-style exploded diagram generator — rejected immediately as a repeat of past ideas Figures and Partsy.
8. Bookmark Shelf — your X bookmarks rendered as a browsable shelf. DROPPED: Granted (@yashsharma_f) is literally this week's bookmark-agent launch; building a thin neighbour of a bookmarked project is against the brief.
9. Changelog Tide — weekly diff of what the top 50 open models can now do in-browser. DROPPED AT SCREEN: good reason to return, but it's a newsletter with a UI; no personal input, nothing to post.
10. Caption Loop — real-time webcam captioning with LFM3-VL WebGPU. DROPPED: the webml-community space and the r/LocalLLaMA video-captioning demo already exist; cloning a published demo.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3/3): Web Summary on ploid.com (confirmed real pricing — $200/mo Growth, 1,000 credits, 25 credits for a deep person lookup — which killed the "people data is now cents" framing as a venture angle for this builder); on a16z's New Security Agenda (gave real CISO numbers: 46% fear agents exceeding permissions, 45% plan to buy internal-agent security within 12 months, 87% expect budget growth — this is what elevated candidate 7 to finalist); on Explee (confirmed $0.04/email pay-as-you-go, which showed how commoditised AI outbound already is and sank candidates 3 and 4).

Screening pot (6/6): agentic identity/NHI governance (found the "Okta + SailPoint for agents" category already forming); city permitting (found CivCheck live in Honolulu and piloted in Seattle, distributed by Clariti — killed candidate 9); Copilot adoption/shelfware (found CloudNuro, LicenseIQ, VisualSP — killed candidate 5); GDPR/data-broker angle (returned nothing usable); deal desk / CPQ (found DealHub, Conga, Salesbricks, Salesforce all routing non-standard terms — demoted candidate 6); benefits income verification (found Plaid Income, SteadyIQ, Argyle, Code for America — pushed me off the income-verification wedge and toward exemptions).

Deep research pot (12/12): spent almost entirely on the Medicaid work-requirement finalist. Established the deadline and scale (KFF tracker, CBO ~5.3M more uninsured by 2034, Urban ~3.1M fewer enrollees year one, Nebraska/Montana/Arkansas/Iowa already moving); mapped the vendor landscape on both ends (Fortuna Health $22M a16z-backed, Healthy Together, Vimo, Centauri, Ushur, mPulse, Pointcare, Relay, Deloitte via KFF) and confirmed none sells the provider-side clinical packet; found the CMS IFR's two-part medically-frail test and the three-tier framework; found Kentucky's MACE-200 and the 30-day cure process; found SHVS's 8 Oct 2026 roadmap telling states to publish standardised provider attestation forms; found an independent analyst explicitly naming the clinician-review tier as unbuilt. Two calls were spent trying and failing to get clinic-level burden and revenue numbers — that failure is why pain stayed at 8.

Sharpening pot (5/5): sized the behavioural-health buyer (495 CCBHCs / ~3M clients; 2,112 OTPs, >600k patients/yr, ~75% Medicaid; Medicare OTP weekly methadone bundle $277.29; KFF $1,609 Medicaid revenue per health-centre patient/yr), checked behavioural-health SaaS price points ($35-$150 per clinician per month, $0.38/claim) to see whether a per-clinic price is normal, and probed multi-state form availability (confirmed Kentucky, could not confirm Montana/Nebraska/Iowa/Indiana — which is why v1 is one state).

Investor signals weighed: YC [latest] "Plaid for Government Benefits" (Alströmer) aimed me at benefits paperwork and I took the narrow provider-side wedge inside it rather than the signal itself; YC [latest] "AI for City Hall" produced candidate 9, killed by CivCheck; YC [latest] "The $15-an-Hour Expert" shaped the product's form (a non-specialist assembling a packet a clinician signs); a16z [latest] "Vertical AI ... to multiplayer" and "AI reinforces business models" supported the provider-revenue framing; a16z's CISO post produced candidate 7. The signals raised timing, not pain or market_pull — those rest on the CMS rule and the state forms I verified myself.
Sharpening (7.4 to 8): Round 1 — weakest criterion: gap (6) and market_pull (6). The original finalist was a generic "Medicaid work-requirement compliance helper for FQHCs and CBOs". Research showed that lane is crowded on both ends: Fortuna Health ($22M, a16z Bio+Health) owns member navigation; Healthy Together and Vimo ship member/state hour-logging and exemption screening (CBPP vendor landscape); Centauri, Ushur, mPulse, Pointcare own payer-side retention outreach. Change to the idea: drop member navigation entirely and move the wedge to the one step none of them touch — the clinician-signed medically-frail packet built from the chart. Evidence found: CMS's IFR makes medical frailty a two-part functional test, not a diagnosis lookup; an independent analyst states the clinician-review tier is unserved and frames it as a layer to sell alongside Fortuna rather than against it; my search for a provider-side exemption documentation vendor returned none. gap 6 → 8, market_pull 6 → 7 (buyer named, but I still have no signed price).

Round 2 — weakest remaining: market_pull (7) and wedge (6). Change: narrow the buyer from "FQHCs and CBOs" to safety-net behavioural health — CCBHCs and OTPs — because their patients map almost one-to-one onto the SUD/SMI frailty categories, they have a single ops/compliance buyer, and the revenue-at-risk argument is sharp. Then narrow the first version to one state with a published provider form. Evidence found: Kentucky already publishes MACE-200 with a provider-signature version and accepts a letterhead attestation; SHVS's 8 Oct 2026 roadmap directs non-self-attestation states to finalise standardised provider attestation forms; SAMHSA lists 2,112 OTPs (~600k patients/yr) and the National Council 495 CCBHCs; behavioural health clinics already buy $35-$150/clinician/month add-ons, so a per-clinic price is normal. What did NOT survive: I could not find any measured volume of letter requests hitting clinics, any clinic staffing data for this task, or a behavioural-health-specific revenue-per-lost-patient figure — so pain stays at 8 (workaround clearly exists and is manual, but no hours/cost numbers) and wedge rises only to 7, because v1 needs state-specific rule encoding and a clinician trust bar, not a weekend. market_pull 7 held (named role, known price points, but no confirmed buyer). Average before sharpening 7.4 → after 8.0.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): Perplexity on LFM3 open weights and browser viability; on nicobailon/skill-diet (which killed candidate 2 — the real tool already does the evaluation loop properly, so a web clone would be worse); on ploid.com pricing, which surfaced the $2.50-per-person-report wall and killed candidate 3. Screening pot (5/5): one search each on SKILL.md token-audit tools (found skill-diet neighbours and ksred/firecrawl commentary — crowded), LFM3 browser support (found the webml-community WebGPU space, which both confirmed the capability and killed candidate 10 as a clone), digital-footprint tools (Whitebridge.ai and a pile of OSINT agents — crowded), AI-sales-agent data tools (saturated), and LFM3-Omni browser support (no demonstrated ONNX browser path yet — killed candidate 4). Deep research (8/8): d1-2B economics and hosting (no confirmed free hosted tier → candidate 5 out); two searches on still-image redaction, which found a dozen free tools (datablur.app, folge.me, blur-face.com) and forced the idea off screenshots and onto video, where nothing free and local exists; searches for video secret-detection, which turned up GitLab's pipeline writeup and hosted VideoLens as the only prior art; frame-extraction feasibility (WebCodecs/ffmpeg.wasm, Simon Willison's wasm tools as precedent); and the Tesseract.js + Gitleaks dependency check. What changed: the whole idea moved from "scan a screenshot" (dead, crowded) to "scan the video you're about to post" (open), and the architecture split into a cheap regex pass plus a selective model pass. Sharpening pot (4/4): the "before you post" searches, the build-in-public leak-anecdote searches (which returned general API-key-leak stories but no X-specific evidence — this is why pain_type is latent, not expressed, and why shareability stayed at 7), VideoLens pricing/alternatives, and the Tesseract/Gitleaks confirmation. Not checked and therefore capped: whether LFM3-VL's semantic findings on real screen-recording frames are accurate enough to trust — that is the riskiest assumption and the validation test targets it.
Sharpening (7.2 to 7.6): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (6.5 → 7.5). Problem: a one-shot "scan my video" is a toy you use once. Change to the idea: made the unit of work the launch itself rather than the file — the result screen ends in an exportable clean video plus a "Clean ✅ / N found" badge, so the tool becomes a step in a recurring ritual (every demo video, every launch) rather than a curiosity. Research (searches for a "before you post" demo-video checker, and for existing frame-by-frame privacy scrubbers) found only hosted/cloud VideoLens (https://videolens.io/video-privacy-analyzer), an internal GitLab pipeline writeup (https://about.gitlab.com/blog/how-to-detecting-secrets-in-video/) and a face-only Python pipeline (https://github.com/kabir0st/automated-video-privacy-pipeline) — nothing occupying the repeat-use, zero-upload slot. Score before 7.2, after 7.4.
Round 2 — weak criterion: buildability (7 → 8). Problem: "run a VLM over every frame of a video in the browser" was an unchecked claim and would be slow. Change to the idea: split into a fast OCR+Gitleaks-regex pass that runs immediately and a selective LFM3-VL pass only on flagged/sampled frames, with the model download non-blocking. Research confirmed every dependency: Tesseract.js is pure-JS in-browser OCR (https://tesseract.projectnaptha.com/), the Gitleaks regex corpus is open (https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks), and LFM3-VL-2B-ONNX q4f16 is ~1.69 GB and runs via Transformers.js v4.3.2+ with a live WebGPU space (https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B-ONNX, https://huggingface.co/spaces/webml-community/LFM3-VL-2B-WebGPU). Freshness held but capped at 7.5 rather than 9, because the honest core (OCR + regex over frames) has been possible for years and only the semantic pass is new; the LFM Open License also has a commercial-use limitation I could not fully clear, which is fine for a free OSS tool but worth noting. Score before 7.4, after 7.6.
prototype_summary: A clickable provider-side Medicaid exemption desk prototype that turns a messy behavioural-health chart into a signed, criteria-mapped MACE-200 exemption packet with citation chips linking every clinical claim back to the source chart line.
